ai.definition: Nuclear fusion is a process in which atomic nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing vast amounts of energy. In a fusion reactor, this process mimics the conditions inside stars like the sun, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium under extreme temperatures and pressures.
ai.howItWorks: Fusion reactors heat plasma (ionized gas) to temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius using various techniques such as magnetic confinement or inertial confinement. The high temperature causes deuterium and tritium isotopes of hydrogen to undergo fusion, producing helium and releasing energy in the form of neutrons and gamma radiation.
ai.problemSolved: Fusion power addresses the global challenge of providing a sustainable, low-carbon source of energy that could replace fossil fuels. It promises virtually unlimited fuel supply from seawater and minimal waste with short-lived radioactive byproducts.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing fusion reactors involves complex engineering challenges such as developing materials resistant to extreme temperatures and radiation, designing efficient magnetic confinement systems or laser-based inertial fusion systems, and integrating advanced control systems.
ai.buildProcess: The build process begins with selecting a reactor design (tokamak, stellarator, laser-fusion), followed by detailed engineering, component fabrication, assembly, testing, and commissioning. Each step requires specialized equipment and expertise.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include the high initial capital investment for research and development, advanced materials, complex manufacturing processes, and long-term operational costs for maintaining reactor integrity and safety systems.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Despite decades of research, fusion power remains in the experimental phase with no commercial reactors yet built. Current projects aim to demonstrate net energy gain within the next decade, but widespread deployment is not expected before mid-century or later.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for fusion power are still evolving. Existing nuclear regulations may apply, requiring stringent safety standards and environmental impact assessments. Specific regulations will depend on national policies and international agreements.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving net energy gain, developing materials that can withstand extreme conditions, and ensuring reactor safety. Economic risks involve the high cost of R&D and potential delays in commercialization. Environmental risks are minimal due to low-level radioactive waste from deuterium-tritium fusion.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the current state of research and lack of commercial-scale deployment. Break-even points for fusion power plants could be decades away, depending on technological advancements and policy support.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will focus on improving reactor designs, reducing costs through economies of scale, advancing materials science, and addressing safety concerns. International collaboration is likely to accelerate progress in this field.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of megawatts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and high-temperature operations.

glossary.def: A stable isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron, used as a fuel in fusion reactors.
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons, also used as a fusion fuel. It can be produced from lithium-6 through neutron capture.
An ionized gas composed of free electrons and ions, often used in fusion reactors to contain the reaction.
A toroidal-shaped device that uses magnetic fields to confine plasma for nuclear fusion reactions. It is one of the leading designs for practical fusion power generation.
Another type of fusion reactor design that uses a complex, non-circular magnetic field configuration to confine plasma without an external current drive.

subsystems.name: Confinement device
subsystems.role: holds the fusing fuel long enough for reactions to outpace losses — either magnetic (tokamak, stellarator) or inertial (laser or pulsed compression).
parts: superconducting magnet coils or high-power laser drivers

subsystems.name: Heating and fuelling
subsystems.role: drives the fuel to fusion temperature and keeps it supplied.

subsystems.name: Blanket and first wall
subsystems.role: the innermost structure: absorbs neutron energy, breeds tritium from lithium, shields the magnets.
parts: lithium-bearing breeder (solid ceramic or liquid metal)

subsystems.name: Exhaust
subsystems.role: removes helium 'ash' and waste heat from the plasma edge so the reaction does not poison itself.

subsystems.name: Tritium fuel cycle
subsystems.role: recovers bred tritium, separates it from other gases and returns it to the fuel supply.

subsystems.name: Balance of plant
subsystems.role: turns captured heat into grid electricity.

subsystems.name: Remote maintenance
subsystems.role: allows components to be replaced without people entering a neutron-activated machine.

buildSteps.title: Pick a confinement route
buildSteps.detail: Magnetic confinement squeezes a low-density plasma for seconds to minutes; inertial confinement compresses a tiny fuel capsule in nanoseconds.

buildSteps.title: Build the driver
buildSteps.detail: Either wind and cool many tonnes of superconducting coil, or assemble a laser or pulsed-power facility delivering megajoules in billionths of a second.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chamber
buildSteps.detail: A torus or target chamber is welded to tight tolerances, with hundreds of ports for heating, fuelling and instruments.

buildSteps.title: Line the inside
buildSteps.detail: First-wall armour, blanket modules and divertor targets are fitted — the parts that face the neutrons, which no fusion device has yet operated with at power-plant duty.

buildSteps.title: Make a burning plasma
buildSteps.detail: Deuterium–tritium fuel is introduced, and the aim is alpha-particle self-heating that keeps the plasma hot largely by itself.

buildSteps.title: Breed the fuel
buildSteps.detail: Lithium blankets must convert neutron collisions into tritium faster than the plant burns it — the fuel cycle is what makes fusion sustainable.

buildSteps.title: Extract the heat
buildSteps.detail: Coolant carries blanket heat to exchangers and a turbine, which no fusion machine has yet done.

buildSteps.title: Operate and maintain remotely
buildSteps.detail: Blanket and divertor modules are designed for robotic replacement on a schedule, because neutron damage will make them radioactive.

prerequisites.why: laser fusion produced more energy than the laser delivered in 2022, and magnetic devices set energy records, but no reactor has produced sustained net gain.
tritium occurs naturally only in trace amounts, so a power plant must manufacture its own fuel from lithium.
fusion neutrons displace atoms in steel far faster than fission neutrons, and no qualified structural material exists for decades of service.

prerequisites.tech: High-field superconducting magnets or high-average-power lasers
prerequisites.why: they set the size and cost of any reactor, and both have been demonstrated only at experimental scale.
commercially viable availability depends on fast robotic replacement of heavily irradiated parts.

pathway.milestone: large magnetic-confinement experiments such as ITER in France, and laser facilities forming burning plasmas
pathway.unlocks: data on self-heating, exhaust and control at reactor-relevant scale.

pathway.milestone: compact high-field tokamaks and other designs targeting fusion gain well above one in smaller machines
pathway.unlocks: a cheaper, faster route to a pilot power plant.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants that deliver electricity to a grid and close the tritium cycle
pathway.unlocks: proof that the whole system — fuel, materials, heat, maintenance — works together.
firm low-carbon baseload power, provided materials and fuel self-sufficiency are solved.
